1) Caustic (chemical) ingestion/aspiration injury to the larynx and supraglottis — Most likely. Diffuse supraglottic mucosal edema with sloughing (epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds) is characteristic of chemical burns (alkali > acid) to pharynx/larynx. Unwitnessed fall with possible loss of consciousness raises the possibility of accidental ingestion/aspiration of a household or industrial corrosive.

2) Thermal inhalation injury (hot gas/steam or smoke inhalation) — Probable. Thermal injury can produce diffuse supraglottic edema and mucosal sloughing; consider if the fall was associated with a fire/exposure.

3) Acute bacterial supraglottitis/epiglottitis with mucosal necrosis — Possible. Acute epiglottitis classically causes severe epiglottic and supraglottic swelling that can obstruct view of the cords; severe infection or delayed presentation can cause mucosal breakdown/sloughing.

4) Blunt laryngeal trauma with mucosal contusion/ischemic necrosis — Possible. Even without fracture on CT, blunt neck trauma can cause mucosal injury and progressive edema/sloughing leading to airway compromise.

5) Angioedema (allergic or drug-induced, e.g., ACE inhibitor) — Less likely. Explains rapid supraglottic edema and airway obstruction but is less consistent with mucosal sloughing and the distribution of injury seen on laryngoscopy.

Key immediate management priorities (already likely underway): definitive airway protection (tracheostomy or secure endotracheal airway), ENT/Airway surgeon involvement, humidified oxygen and airway suctioning, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics if infection suspected, supportive care. Important next diagnostic steps to differentiate causes: targeted history for exposures/ingestions, toxicology/caustic agent identification, bronchoscopy/airway endoscopy for distal airway assessment, culture/blood tests if infection suspected.
